Find the log-likelihood function of the sample." :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

We are given a sample of $n=10$ independent Bernoulli random variables with unknown parameter $\theta.$ Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
f(x;\theta) = \theta^x(1-\theta)^{1-x}, \qquad x=0, 1.
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{1-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{1-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(1-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(1-{x}_{i}) \\  & =S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $\displaystyle S = \sum_ {i=1}^n x_i$ is the number of successes in the sample.

Finally, since there are $7$ successes in the sample, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =7\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(10-7)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =7\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192795 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-4f0ef3b3-16ee-5e79-a46a-c889944b927a" "question-ca066a36-cc0e-5545-b489-303cc36ed2ab" "question-a772fd34-b53c-57c2-a042-bacdd3f39061" "question-aac7d9dd-e1f6-55a0-8d3e-a363440ea2a6" "question-39034469-ded2-572d-9811-0121a992e366"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192519 :question/problem "Suppose $X_1, X_2, X_3$ is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i \sim B(5,\theta)$ with unknown probability of success $\theta.$ You're given the particular sample 

$$
x_1 = 4, \qquad x_2 = 1, \qquad x_3 = 1.
$$

Find the log-likelihood function of this sample.

*Hint: The probability mass function for a binomial random variable is given by*

$$
f(x) = \displaystyle \binom{5}{x} \theta^x (1-\theta)^{5-x}, \qquad x = 0,1, \ldots, 5.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n = 3$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta$ and $N = 5$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{5-x},\,x=0,1,…,5.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{5-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{5-{x}_{i}})) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(5-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(5-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(5n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $\displaystyle S = \sum_ {i=1}^n x_i.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{3}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta)$ becomes

$$
l(\theta) =  \ln\left( \prod_{i=1}^n {5 \choose x_i}\right) + S\ln \theta + (5n - S) \ln(1-\theta).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{4})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{1}) \\  & =5\cdot 5\cdot 5 \\  & =125,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
S = 4 + 1 + 1 = 6.
$$

Substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta)$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(125)+6\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(5\cdot 3-6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡125+6\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +9\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192796 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d978fa3e-6005-512f-876c-9fe43876b042" "question-766020c7-f3e3-5fda-b856-3ebb3916a4d5" "question-9585d3de-f669-5f4a-af08-1394e7187c1e" "question-feffea6d-5c4c-51cd-843c-44b1eafaf816" "question-680ba03b-6073-56c3-bf2a-b6b3fb6a93d2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192520 :question/problem "Suppose $X_1,X_2,X_3$ is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i\sim \mathrm{Po}(\theta)$ with unknown rate parameter $\theta.$ You're given the particular sample

$$
x_1 = 3,\qquad x_2=4,\qquad x_3 = 1.
$$

Find the log-likelihood function of the sample." :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=3$ independent Poisson random variables with unknown parameter $\theta.$ Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & ={e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{x}}{x!}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}}{{x}_{i}!}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta })+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}1+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-n\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}!)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}! & =3!\cdot 4!\cdot 1!=6\cdot 24\cdot 1=144, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =3+4+1=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-3\theta +8\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\operatorname{ln}⁡144.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-5c38f1db-70a0-5329-a7b6-a10067496307" :question/id #uuid "5c38f1db-70a0-5329-a7b6-a10067496307" :question/math-academy-id "q-159869" :question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{7}$ is an I.I.D random sample where ${X}_{i}∼\text{Bernoulli}(\theta )$ with unknown probability of success $\theta .$ For a particular sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{7},$ you're given that there are $3$ successes. $$

We are given a sample of $n=7$ independent Bernoulli random variables with unknown parameter $\theta .$ Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$

Finally, since there are $3$ successes in the sample, we have

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

We are given a sample of $n=15$ independent Bernoulli random variables with unknown parameter $\theta .$ Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
f(x;\theta )={\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{1-x},\,x=0,1.
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{1-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{1-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(1-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(1-{x}_{i}) \\  & =S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}$ is the number of successes in the sample.

Finally, since there are $6$ successes in the sample, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(15-6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +9\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=3$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=6$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{6-x},\,x=0,1,…,6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{6-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{6-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(6-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(6-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(6n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{3}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta )$ becomes

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}}))+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(6n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{2})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{5})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{6}) \\  & =15\cdot 6\cdot 1 \\  & =90,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
S=2+5+6=13.
$$

Substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta )$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(90)+13\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(6\cdot 3-13)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(90)+13\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +5\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=90+13+5=108.

${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3},{X}_{4}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼B(7,\theta )$ with unknown probability of success $\theta .$ You're given the particular sample 

$$
{x}_{1}=6,\,{x}_{2}=1,\,{x}_{3}=2,\,{x}_{4}=7.
$$

The log-likelihood function of the sample is given by

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡a+b\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +c\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$

*Hint: The probability mass function for a binomial random variable is given by*

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{7-x},\,x=0,1,…,7.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=7$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{7-x},\,x=0,1,…,7.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{7-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{7-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(7-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(7-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(7n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{3}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{4}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta )$ becomes

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}}))+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(7n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{6})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{2})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{7}) \\  & =7\cdot 7\cdot 21\cdot 1 \\  & =1\,029,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
S=6+1+2+7=16.
$$

Substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta )$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\,029)+16\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(7\cdot 4-16)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1\,029+16\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +12\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=1\,029+16+12=1\,057.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a5ebfda0-c699-5d31-9e1a-8c1a1852116a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=3$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=5$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{5-x},\,x=0,1,…,5.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{5-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{5-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(5-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(5-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(5n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{3}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta )$ becomes

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}))+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(5n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{5})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{3})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{2}) \\  & =1\cdot 10\cdot 10 \\  & =100,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
S=5+3+2=10.

Substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta )$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(100)+10\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(5\cdot 3-10)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(100)+10\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +5\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=100+10+5=115.

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=4$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{4-x},\,x=0,1,2,3,4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{4-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{4-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(4-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(4-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(4n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{3}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{4}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta )$ becomes

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}))+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(4n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{2})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{3}) \\  & =4\cdot 6\cdot 4\cdot 4 \\  & =384,\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
{x}_{1}=1,\,{x}_{2}=1,\,{x}_{3}=0,\,{x}_{4}=4.
$$

The log-likelihood function of the sample is given by

$$
l(\theta )=a\theta +b\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\operatorname{ln}⁡c.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent Poisson random variables with unknown parameter $\theta .$ Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & ={e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{x}}{x!}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}}{{x}_{i}!}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta })+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}1+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-n\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}!)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}! & =1!\cdot 1!\cdot 0!\cdot 4!=1\cdot 1\cdot 1\cdot 24=24, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =1+1+0+4=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-4\theta +6\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\operatorname{ln}⁡24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=-4+6+24=26.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a48845ac-16bf-54fa-96e4-0933e3531df9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id \begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent Poisson random variables with unknown parameter $\theta .$ Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & ={e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{x}}{x!}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}}{{x}_{i}!}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta })+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}1+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-n\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}!)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}! & =3!\cdot 2!\cdot 1!\cdot 5!=6\cdot 2\cdot 1\cdot 120=1\,440, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =3+2+1+5=11.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-4\theta +11\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\operatorname{ln}⁡1\,440.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=-4+11+1\,440=1\,447.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-22f32989-72b2-5437-9672-f47842734fbb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-22f32989-72b2-5437-9672-f47842734fbb" :answer-field/id #uuid "22f32989-72b2-5437-9672-f47842734fbb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-725d6c8e-de45-5da8-bf6d-00039ba4a5a2" :answer-field/choices ["answer-725d6c8e-de45-5da8-bf6d-00039ba4a5a2" "answer-61625b6e-fafc-5735-99c7-51bacdd3efaa" "answer-5b6624e9-ff65-58e4-bb1a-cbc97c080b3a" "answer-6729961d-5125-51e3-9441-2b4cea93a506" "answer-5227129a-cf10-5014-b945-9b282b56a162"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-725d6c8e-de45-5da8-bf6d-00039ba4a5a2" :answer/id #uuid "725d6c8e-de45-5da8-bf6d-00039ba4a5a2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1\,447" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-61625b6e-fafc-5735-99c7-51bacdd3efaa" :answer/id #uuid "61625b6e-fafc-5735-99c7-51bacdd3efaa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1\,465" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5b6624e9-ff65-58e4-bb1a-cbc97c080b3a" :answer/id #uuid "5b6624e9-ff65-58e4-bb1a-cbc97c080b3a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "432" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6729961d-5125-51e3-9441-2b4cea93a506" :answer/id #uuid "6729961d-5125-51e3-9441-2b4cea93a506" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "727" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5227129a-cf10-5014-b945-9b282b56a162" :answer/id #uuid "5227129a-cf10-5014-b945-9b282b56a162" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "743" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193898 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $X_1, \: X_2, \: \ldots, \: X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, \: x_2, \: \ldots, \: x_n$ is 

$$
L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).
$$

For example, if 

$$
X_1,\quad X_2,\quad X_3,\quad X_4,\quad X_5,\quad X_6
$$

is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i\sim \text{Bernoulli}(\theta),$ where $\theta$ is the unknown probability of success, then the likelihood function of the sample 

$$
x_1=0, \quad x_2=1, \quad x_3=1, \quad x_4=0, \quad x_5=1, \quad x_6=1
$$

 

is given by 

$$
L(\theta) = \theta^{4}(1-\theta)^{2}.
$$

The likelihood function contains lots of products, which can be cumbersome to work with. To make things easier, we convert the products into sums by finding the natural logarithm of $L(\theta),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(L(\theta )) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta )) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{1};\,\theta )\cdot f({x}_{2};\,\theta )⋯f({x}_{n};\,\theta )) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{1};\,\theta ))+\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{2};\,\theta ))+⋯+\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{n};\,\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\,\theta ))\end{aligned}
$$

This new function $l(\theta)$ is called the **log-likelihood function** of the sample.

For our Bernoulli example above, the corresponding log-likelihood function is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{4}(1-\theta )^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{4})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{2}) \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193901 :tutorial/content "The graph of the likelihood function 

$$
L(\theta) = \theta^4(1\!-\!\theta)^2
$$

for the Bernoulli distribution we saw earlier is shown below. 

![](images/28/28c73749a566d5531ef2f13c5b01bd1d26ced28e19749abf056841492fb497f5.png)

The graph of the corresponding log-likelihood function

$$
l(\theta) = 4 \ln \theta + 2 \ln(1-\theta)
$$

is shown below.

![](images/f7/f7f0ba3147504869e162dd371f98d5d6c492e89345f80c75037bdc82a6006d1c.png)

Although the graphs look quite different, they both have a maximum at the same point $\theta = \widehat{\,\theta\,}.$ This will become important later. 

Let's see more examples of finding the log-likelihood functions for different distributions and samples." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192933 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{1-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{1-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(1-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(1-{x}_{i}) \\  & =S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}

$$

Find the log-likelihood function of this sample.

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n = 3$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta$ and $N = 5$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{5-x},\,x=0,1,…,5.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{5-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{5-{x}_{i}})) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(5-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(5-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(5n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $\displaystyle S = \sum_ {i=1}^n x_i.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{3}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta)$ becomes

$$

$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{4})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{1}) \\  & =5\cdot 5\cdot 5 \\  & =125,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
S = 4 + 1 + 1 = 6.
$$

Substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta)$, we get

$$

probability of success $\theta .$ You're given the particular sample 

$$
{x}_{1}=2,\,{x}_{2}=5,\,{x}_{3}=6.
$$

The log-likelihood function of the sample is given by

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡a+b\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +c\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=3$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=6$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{6-x},\,x=0,1,…,6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{6-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{6-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(6-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(6-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(6n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{3}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta )$ becomes

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}}))+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(6n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{2})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{5})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{6}) \\  & =15\cdot 6\cdot 1 \\  & =90,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
S=2+5+6=13.
$$

an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼B(4,\theta )$ with unknown probability of success $\theta .$ You're given the particular sample 

$$
{x}_{1}=1,\,{x}_{2}=2,\,{x}_{3}=3,\,{x}_{4}=4,\,{x}_{5}=4,\,{x}_{6}=3.
$$

The log-likelihood function of the sample is given by

l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡a+b\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +c\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=6$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=4$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{4-x},\,x=0,1,…,4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{4-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{4-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(4-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(4-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(4n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{3}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{4}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{5}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{6}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta )$ becomes

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}))+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(4n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{2})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{3})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{4})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{4})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{3}) \\  & =4\cdot 6\cdot 4\cdot 1\cdot 1\cdot 4 \\  & =384,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
S=1+2+3+4+4+3=17.
$$

Substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta )$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(384)+17\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(4\cdot 6-17)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(384)+17\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +7\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=384+17+7=408.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-99390f67-0220-5a26-b39c-6b99ee5db62a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=7$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{7-x},\,x=0,1,…,7.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{7-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{7-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(7-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(7-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(7n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{3}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{4}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta )$ becomes

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}}))+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(7n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{6})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{2})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{7}) \\  & =7\cdot 7\cdot 21\cdot 1 \\  & =1\,029,\end{aligned}

and

$$
S=6+1+2+7=16.

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\,029)+16\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(7\cdot 4-16)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1\,029+16\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +12\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}

Finally,

$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=3$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=5$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{5-x},\,x=0,1,…,5.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{5-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{5-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(5-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(5-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(5n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{3}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta )$ becomes

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}))+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(5n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{5})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{3})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{2}) \\  & =1\cdot 10\cdot 10 \\  & =100,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
S=5+3+2=10.

Substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta )$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(100)+10\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(5\cdot 3-10)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(100)+10\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +5\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=100+10+5=115.

$$
{x}_{1}=1,\,{x}_{2}=2,\,{x}_{3}=1,\,{x}_{4}=3.
$$

The log-likelihood function of the sample is given by

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡a+b\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +c\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$

*Hint: The probability mass function for a binomial random variable is given by*

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{4-x},\,x=0,1,2,3,4.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=4$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{4-x},\,x=0,1,2,3,4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{4-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{4-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(4-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(4-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(4n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{3}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{4}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta )$ becomes

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}))+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(4n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{2})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{3}) \\  & =4\cdot 6\cdot 4\cdot 4 \\  & =384,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
S=1+2+1+3=7.
$$

Substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta )$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(384)+7\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(4\cdot 4-7)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡384+7\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +9\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=384+7+9=400.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cb00ed38-5141-52cf-9136-8d37b807205f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent Poisson random variables with unknown parameter $\theta .$ Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & ={e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{x}}{x!}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}}{{x}_{i}!}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta })+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}1+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-n\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}!)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}! & =1!\cdot 1!\cdot 0!\cdot 4!=1\cdot 1\cdot 1\cdot 24=24, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =1+1+0+4=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-4\theta +6\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\operatorname{ln}⁡24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=-4+6+24=26.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a48845ac-16bf-54fa-96e4-0933e3531df9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-feffea6d-5c4c-51cd-843c-44b1eafaf816" :question/id #uuid "feffea6d-5c4c-51cd-843c-44b1eafaf816" :question/math-academy-id "q-159848" :question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3},{X}_{4}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼Po(\theta )$ with unknown rate parameter $\theta .$ You're given the particular sample

$$
{x}_{1}=0,\,{x}_{2}=2,\,{x}_{3}=5,\,{x}_{4}=1.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent Poisson random variables with unknown parameter $\theta .$ Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & ={e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{x}}{x!}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}}{{x}_{i}!}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta })+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}1+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-n\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}!)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}! & =0!\cdot 2!\cdot 5!\cdot 1!=1\cdot 2\cdot 120\cdot 1=240, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =0+2+5+1=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-4\theta +8\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\operatorname{ln}⁡240.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=-4+8+240=244.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-84290a67-87f1-59fd-a0d4-ccc92cc9e83d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent Poisson random variables with unknown parameter $\theta .$ Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & ={e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{x}}{x!}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}}{{x}_{i}!}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta })+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}1+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-n\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}!)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}! & =3!\cdot 2!\cdot 1!\cdot 5!=6\cdot 2\cdot 1\cdot 120=1\,440, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =3+2+1+5=11.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-4\theta +11\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\operatorname{ln}⁡1\,440.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=-4+11+1\,440=1\,447.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-22f32989-72b2-5437-9672-f47842734fbb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-22f32989-72b2-5437-9672-f47842734fbb" :answer-field/id #uuid "22f32989-72b2-5437-9672-f47842734fbb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-725d6c8e-de45-5da8-bf6d-00039ba4a5a2" :answer-field/choices ["answer-725d6c8e-de45-5da8-bf6d-00039ba4a5a2" "answer-61625b6e-fafc-5735-99c7-51bacdd3efaa" "answer-5b6624e9-ff65-58e4-bb1a-cbc97c080b3a" "answer-6729961d-5125-51e3-9441-2b4cea93a506" "answer-5227129a-cf10-5014-b945-9b282b56a162"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-725d6c8e-de45-5da8-bf6d-00039ba4a5a2" :answer/id #uuid "725d6c8e-de45-5da8-bf6d-00039ba4a5a2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1\,447" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-61625b6e-fafc-5735-99c7-51bacdd3efaa" :answer/id #uuid "61625b6e-fafc-5735-99c7-51bacdd3efaa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1\,465" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5b6624e9-ff65-58e4-bb1a-cbc97c080b3a" :answer/id #uuid "5b6624e9-ff65-58e4-bb1a-cbc97c080b3a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "432" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6729961d-5125-51e3-9441-2b4cea93a506" :answer/id #uuid "6729961d-5125-51e3-9441-2b4cea93a506" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "727" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5227129a-cf10-5014-b945-9b282b56a162" :answer/id #uuid "5227129a-cf10-5014-b945-9b282b56a162" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "743" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193898 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $X_1, \: X_2, \: \ldots, \: X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, \: x_2, \: \ldots, \: x_n$ is 

$$
L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).
$$

For example, if 

$$
X_1,\quad X_2,\quad X_3,\quad X_4,\quad X_5,\quad X_6
$$

is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i\sim \text{Bernoulli}(\theta),$ where $\theta$ is the unknown probability of success, then the likelihood function of the sample 

$$
x_1=0, \quad x_2=1, \quad x_3=1, \quad x_4=0, \quad x_5=1, \quad x_6=1
$$

 

is given by 

$$
L(\theta) = \theta^{4}(1-\theta)^{2}.
$$

The likelihood function contains lots of products, which can be cumbersome to work with. To make things easier, we convert the products into sums by finding the natural logarithm of $L(\theta),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(L(\theta )) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta )) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{1};\,\theta )\cdot f({x}_{2};\,\theta )⋯f({x}_{n};\,\theta )) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{1};\,\theta ))+\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{2};\,\theta ))+⋯+\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{n};\,\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\,\theta ))\end{aligned}
$$

This new function $l(\theta)$ is called the **log-likelihood function** of the sample.

For our Bernoulli example above, the corresponding log-likelihood function is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{4}(1-\theta )^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{4})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{2}) \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193901 :tutorial/content "The graph of the likelihood function 

$$
L(\theta) = \theta^4(1\!-\!\theta)^2
$$

for the Bernoulli distribution we saw earlier is shown below. 

![](images/28/28c73749a566d5531ef2f13c5b01bd1d26ced28e19749abf056841492fb497f5.png)

The graph of the corresponding log-likelihood function

$$
l(\theta) = 4 \ln \theta + 2 \ln(1-\theta)
$$

is shown below.

![](images/f7/f7f0ba3147504869e162dd371f98d5d6c492e89345f80c75037bdc82a6006d1c.png)

Although the graphs look quite different, they both have a maximum at the same point $\theta = \widehat{\,\theta\,}.$ This will become important later.

Find the log-likelihood function of the sample."] [17592186192390 :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i};\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

We are given a sample of $n=10$ independent Bernoulli random variables with unknown parameter $\theta.$ Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
f(x;\theta) = \theta^x(1-\theta)^{1-x}, \qquad x=0, 1.
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{1-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{1-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(1-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(1-{x}_{i}) \\  & =S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $\displaystyle S = \sum_ {i=1}^n x_i$ is the number of successes in the sample.

Finally, since there are $7$ successes in the sample, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =7\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(10-7)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =7\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186192519 :question/problem "Suppose $X_1, X_2, X_3$ is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i \sim B(5,\theta)$ with unknown probability of success $\theta.$ You're given the particular sample

$$"] [17592186192519 :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x; \theta),$ where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n = 3$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta$ and $N = 5$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{5-x},\,x=0,1,…,5.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{5-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{5-{x}_{i}})) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(5-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(5-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(5n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $\displaystyle S = \sum_ {i=1}^n x_i.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{3}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta)$ becomes

$$
l(\theta) =  \ln\left( \prod_{i=1}^n {5 \choose x_i}\right) + S\ln \theta + (5n - S) \ln(1-\theta).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{4})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{1}) \\  & =5\cdot 5\cdot 5 \\  & =125,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
S = 4 + 1 + 1 = 6.
$$

Substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta)$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(125)+6\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(5\cdot 3-6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡125+6\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +9\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186192520 :question/problem "Suppose $X_1,X_2,X_3$ is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i\sim \mathrm{Po}(\theta)$ with unknown rate parameter $\theta.$ You're given the particular sample

$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=3$ independent Poisson random variables with unknown parameter $\theta.$ Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & ={e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{x}}{x!}.\end{aligned}

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}}{{x}_{i}!}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta })+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}1+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-n\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}!)\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=3$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=6$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{6-x},\,x=0,1,…,6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{6-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{6-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(6-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(6-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(6n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{3}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta )$ becomes

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}}))+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(6n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{2})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{5})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{6}) \\  & =15\cdot 6\cdot 1 \\  & =90,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
S=2+5+6=13.
$$

Substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta )$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(90)+13\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(6\cdot 3-13)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(90)+13\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +5\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=90+13+5=108.

"question-ca066a36-cc0e-5545-b489-303cc36ed2ab"] ["question-a772fd34-b53c-57c2-a042-bacdd3f39061" :question/id #uuid "a772fd34-b53c-57c2-a042-bacdd3f39061"] ["question-a772fd34-b53c-57c2-a042-bacdd3f39061" :question/math-academy-id "q-159893"] ["question-a772fd34-b53c-57c2-a042-bacdd3f39061" :question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3},{X}_{4}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼B(7,\theta )$ with unknown probability of success $\theta .$ You're given the particular sample 

$$
{x}_{1}=6,\,{x}_{2}=1,\,{x}_{3}=2,\,{x}_{4}=7.
$$

The log-likelihood function of the sample is given by

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡a+b\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +c\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$

*Hint: The probability mass function for a binomial random variable is given by*

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{7-x},\,x=0,1,…,7.
$$"] ["question-a772fd34-b53c-57c2-a042-bacdd3f39061" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=7$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{7-x},\,x=0,1,…,7.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{7-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{7-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(7-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(7-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(7n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{3}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{4}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta )$ becomes

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}}))+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(7n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{6})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{2})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{7}) \\  & =7\cdot 7\cdot 21\cdot 1 \\  & =1\,029,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
S=6+1+2+7=16.
$$

Substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta )$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\,029)+16\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(7\cdot 4-16)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1\,029+16\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +12\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=1\,029+16+12=1\,057.
$$"] ["question-a772fd34-b53c-57c2-a042-bacdd3f39061" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-a5ebfda0-c699-5d31-9e1a-8c1a1852116a" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼B(4,\theta )$ with unknown probability of success $\theta .$ You're given the particular sample 

$$
{x}_{1}=1,\,{x}_{2}=2,\,{x}_{3}=1,\,{x}_{4}=3.
$$

The log-likelihood function of the sample is given by

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡a+b\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +c\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$

*Hint: The probability mass function for a binomial random variable is given by*

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{4-x},\,x=0,1,2,3,4.
$$"] ["question-39034469-ded2-572d-9811-0121a992e366" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=4$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{4-x},\,x=0,1,2,3,4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{4-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{4-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(4-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(4-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(4n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{3}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{4}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta )$ becomes

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}))+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(4n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{2})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{3}) \\  & =4\cdot 6\cdot 4\cdot 4 \\  & =384,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
S=1+2+1+3=7.
$$

Substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta )$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(384)+7\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(4\cdot 4-7)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡384+7\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +9\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=384+7+9=400.
$$"] ["question-39034469-ded2-572d-9811-0121a992e366" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-cb00ed38-5141-52cf-9136-8d37b807205f" :answer-field/id #uuid
