$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent Poisson random variables with unknown parameter $\theta .$ Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & ={e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{x}}{x!}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}}{{x}_{i}!}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta })+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}1+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-n\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}!)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}! & =1!\cdot 1!\cdot 0!\cdot 4!=1\cdot 1\cdot 1\cdot 24=24, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =1+1+0+4=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-4\theta +6\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\operatorname{ln}⁡24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=-4+6+24=26.
$$"] ["question-d978fa3e-6005-512f-876c-9fe43876b042" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-a48845ac-16bf-54fa-96e4-0933e3531df9" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=3$ independent Poisson random variables with unknown parameter $\theta .$ Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & ={e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{x}}{x!}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}}{{x}_{i}!}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta })+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}1+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-n\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}!)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}! & =3!\cdot 3!\cdot 2!=6\cdot 6\cdot 2=72, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =3+3+2=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-3\theta +8\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\operatorname{ln}⁡72.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=-3+8+72=77.
$$"] ["question-766020c7-f3e3-5fda-b856-3ebb3916a4d5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-6df3f188-93fa-57a8-a9f9-cc6be388f8c1" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
{x}_{1}=0,\,{x}_{2}=1,\,{x}_{3}=1,\,{x}_{4}=0,\,{x}_{5}=2.
$$

The log-likelihood function of the sample is given by

$$
l(\theta )=a\theta +b\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\operatorname{ln}⁡c.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$

$$"] ["question-9585d3de-f669-5f4a-af08-1394e7187c1e" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=5$ independent Poisson random variables with unknown parameter $\theta .$ Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & ={e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{x}}{x!}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{{x}_{i}}}{{x}_{i}!}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-\theta })+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(-\theta )+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\theta )-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}1+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}_{i}!) \\  & =-n\theta +\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}-\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}!)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}! & =0!\cdot 1!\cdot 1!\cdot 0!\cdot 2!=1\cdot 1\cdot 1\cdot 1\cdot 2=2, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =0+1+1+0+2=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =-5\theta +4\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta -\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=-5+4+2=1.
$$"] ["question-9585d3de-f669-5f4a-af08-1394e7187c1e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-a88b271e-3f4c-50f4-b81d-a23474066dc3" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & ={e}^{-\theta }\cdot \frac{{\theta }^{x}}{x!}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}! & =3!\cdot 2!\cdot 1!\cdot 5!=6\cdot 2\cdot 1\cdot 120=1\,440, \\ {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =3+2+1+5=11.\end{aligned}

$$

\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}

and

$$

Substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta)$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
l(θ) &= \ln (125) + 6\ln θ + (5 \cdot 3 - 6)\ln (1 - θ) \\
&= \ln 125 + 6\ln θ + 9\ln (1 - θ)
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050651} {:db/id 17592186192982 :question/id #uuid "3c5a4f80-f4bc-5f85-966c-3fd9204d967e" :question/math-academy-id "q-143471"} {:db/id 17592186193193 :question/id #uuid "41aee578-0d3b-5160-a35a-432974a0ab73" :question/math-academy-id "q-159771"} {:db/id 17592186192796 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192520 :question/id #uuid "5df5188f-3dfe-599f-b6f3-16b93c433ab1" :question/math-academy-id "e-11120"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a0ab99b4-70b8-5638-bbad-763ef925021c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049358}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186192983 :question/id #uuid "1b44bc46-2ed5-5c39-aeeb-2a4f2782bbaa" :question/math-academy-id "q-143473"} {:db/id 17592186193194 :question/id #uuid "d142c298-92b6-5eb8-b79c-25b9f7c9fa90" :question/math-academy-id "q-159772"}] :knowledge-point/title "Log-Likelihood Functions for Poisson Random Variables"} {:db/id 17592186192520 :question/id #uuid "5df5188f-3dfe-599f-b6f3-16b93c433ab1" :question/math-academy-id "e-11120" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186192796 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a0ab99b4-70b8-5638-bbad-763ef925021c" :knowledge-point/title "Log-Likelihood Functions for Poisson Random Variables"}] :question/problem "Suppose $X_1,X_2,X_3$ is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i\sim \mathrm{Po}(\theta)$ with unknown rate parameter $\theta$. You're given the particular sample
$x_1 = 3,\qquad x_2=4,\qquad x_3 = 1$.

Find the log-likelihood function of the sample." :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x; \theta)$, where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
l(θ) &= \ln L(θ) \\
&= \ln (∏_(i = 1)^(n)f(x_{i}, θ)) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (f(x_{i}, θ))
\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=3$ independent Poisson random variables with unknown parameter $\theta$. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x, θ) &= e^{- θ} \cdot \frac{θ^{x}}{x!}
\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
l(θ) &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (e^{- θ} \cdot \frac{θ^{x_{i}}}{x_{i}!}) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (e^{- θ}) + \ln (θ^{x_{i}}) - \ln (x_{i}!) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(- θ) + ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (θ^{x_{i}}) - ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (x_{i}!) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(- θ) + ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}\ln (θ) - ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (x_{i}!) \\
&= - θ∑_(i = 1)^(n)1 + \ln θ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} - ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (x_{i}!) \\
&=-nθ + \ln θ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} - \ln (∏_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}!)
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=3$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
∏_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}! &= 3! \cdot 4! \cdot 1! = 6 \cdot 24 \cdot 1 = 144, \\
∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} &= 3 + 4 + 1 = 8
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta)$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
l(θ) &= -3θ + 8\ln θ - \ln 144
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049358} {:db/id 17592186192983 :question/id #uuid "1b44bc46-2ed5-5c39-aeeb-2a4f2782bbaa" :question/math-academy-id "q-143473"} {:db/id 17592186193194 :question/id #uuid "d142c298-92b6-5eb8-b79c-25b9f7c9fa90" :question/math-academy-id "q-159772"} {:db/id 17592186049417} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186193682} :activity/id #uuid "e57b078d-2a16-5382-988b-203a38260e4a" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048346 :topic/id #uuid "977d7a77-a9aa-53d4-9b35-0ca8240c298e" :topic/math-academy-id 4124} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186193506 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192685 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192390 :question/id #uuid "3ad1cf25-eb36-5946-9e06-16896691aaea" :question/math-academy-id "e-10112"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ea184595-346e-5c0c-bb95-8779d73f6f6b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048485} {:db/id 17592186048922} {:db/id 17592186049195} {:db/id 17592186051082}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186192981} {:db/id 17592186193192}] :knowledge-point/title "Log-Likelihood Functions for Bernoulli Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "d5b9252a-b7f5-52fe-a10d-b66f5fe665fb" :step/math-academy-id 38134 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193683}} {:db/id 17592186193682 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193898 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $X_1, \: X_2, \: \ldots, \: X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x; \theta)$, where $\theta$ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, \: x_2, \: \ldots, \: x_n$ is

$$
L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta)
$$

For example, if

$X_1,\quad X_2,\quad X_3,\quad X_4,\quad X_5,\quad X_6$
is an I.I.D random sample with $X_i\sim \text{Bernoulli}(\theta)$, where $\theta$ is the unknown probability of success, then the likelihood function of the sample

$$
x_1=0, \quad x_2=1, \quad x_3=1, \quad x_4=0, \quad x_5=1, \quad x_6=1
$$

is given by

$$
L(\theta) = \theta^{4}(1-\theta)^{2}
$$

The likelihood function contains lots of products, which can be cumbersome to work with. To make things easier, we convert the products into sums by finding the natural logarithm of $L(\theta)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
l(θ) &= \ln (L(θ)) \\
&= \ln (∏_(i = 1)^(n)f(x_{i} \\
&= θ)) \\
&= \ln (f(x_{1} \\
&= θ) \cdot f(x_{2} \\
&= θ)⋯f(x_{n} \\
&= θ)) \\
&= \ln (f(x_{1} \\
&= θ)) + \ln (f(x_{2} \\
&= θ)) + ⋯ + \ln (f(x_{n} \\
&= θ)) \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)\ln (f(x_{i} \\
&= θ))
\end{aligned}
$$

This new function $l(\theta)$ is called the **log-likelihood function** of the sample.

For our Bernoulli example above, the corresponding log-likelihood function is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
l(θ) &= \ln (θ^{4}(1 - θ)^{2}) \\
&= \ln (θ^{4}) + \ln ((1 - θ)^{2}) \\
&= 4\ln θ + 2\ln (1 - θ)
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0100980e-b08d-530a-9a07-668209e0af44" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7002 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "13d18ec0-09d2-5510-8edc-00b0f1781b94" :step/math-academy-id 42269 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193691}} {:db/id 17592186193683 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192795 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192519 :question/id #uuid "4d597364-c8aa-5848-843b-bfc870ebe737" :question/math-academy-id "e-11119"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "50df0342-4c06-5c50-90ae-812403a69cee" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050651}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186192982} {:db/id 17592186193193}] :knowledge-point/title "Log-Likelihood Functions for Binomial Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "012bca18-0bfe-527e-a3ee-dcfee75eafd8" :step/math-academy-id 42275 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193684}} {:db/id 17592186193684 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192796 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192520 :question/id #uuid "5df5188f-3dfe-599f-b6f3-16b93c433ab1" :question/math-academy-id "e-11120"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a0ab99b4-70b8-5638-bbad-763ef925021c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049358}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186192983} {:db/id 17592186193194}] :knowledge-point/title "Log-Likelihood Functions for Poisson Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "f297c08f-8ed0-5ea9-a51f-0fdf821d69d8" :step/math-academy-id 42276} {:db/id 17592186193691 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193901 :tutorial/content "The graph of the likelihood function

This new function $l(\theta)$ is called the **log-likelihood function** of the sample.

$$
\begin{aligned}
l(θ) &= \ln (θ^{4}(1 - θ)^{2}) \\
&= \ln (θ^{4}) + \ln ((1 - θ)^{2}) \\
&= 4\ln θ + 2\ln (1 - θ)
\end{aligned}
